title: Tripurantaka: the three cities
hookLine: three flying cities fall to one arrow; why Hindus light lamps on Kartik's full moon, and what Shiva the destroyer destroys
carry: shiva's fire burns what binds the soul
tomorrow: why is that statue half a man and half a woman?

cards: Every contract has a clause somebody hopes nobody will read. Three brothers in the Shiva Purana write theirs very carefully. They are the sons of Taraka, the demon whose boon sent the gods looking for a son of Shiva.
With the marriage done, that son, Kartikeya, has defeated their father. Now the brothers practice tapas in the forest until Brahma, the creator, appears and offers a boon. They ask never to die.
Brahma says no. So they ask for something cleverer.

teach.b: Three cities. Maya, the great builder of the demons, makes them: one of gold in the heavens, one of silver in the sky, one of iron on the earth. And here's the clause.
The cities can be destroyed only when the three come into line, which happens rarely, and only by a single arrow. Never dying, with better paperwork.
The brothers flourish, then turn on the gods, and the gods come to Shiva.

teach.h: THE WHOLE WORLD BECOMES THE CHARIOT.
teach.b: So the gods make him a chariot out of the world itself. The earth is the chariot, the sun and the moon its wheels. Brahma takes the reins.

A mountain is the bow, and Vishnu himself becomes the arrow. When the cities slide into line, Shiva looses it, and all three burn at once. That's why he's called Tripurantaka, the ender of the three cities.
The full moon of Kartik, in autumn, is called Tripuri Purnima, and in Varanasi the riverbanks are lined with lamps, Dev Deepawali, the gods' own Diwali. Then the teachers go deeper.
In South Indian Shaiva teaching, going back to the poet-saint Tirumular, the three cities are read as three bonds that hold a soul: the small, grasping ego, karma, and the pull of the passing world.
Read that way, Shiva's arrow isn't aimed at us, but at what traps us: the grudge that runs you, the pride you can't put down.
That is what Shiva the destroyer destroys, and why teachers call his fire grace.

how: Shiva as Tripurantaka, the ender of the three cities, is retold in the Shiva Purana and shown in temple sculpture with his bow drawn; many Hindus remember the victory on Kartik's full moon, Tripuri Purnima, when Varanasi lines its riverbanks with lamps for Dev Deepawali.

practice: If you can, light a lamp or a candle, the way families do on Kartik's full moon. Name one bond you'd like loosened: a grudge, a pride, a habit that runs you.

Hold it before the flame, and as the breath goes out, say Om Namah Shivaya, or the name of God you use, offering it to the fire. If you don't pray, simply watch the flame and name what you'd like to let go.

wordCard.voice: The Shiva Purana. Today's selection: three flying cities, one arrow, and a chariot made of the whole world. Shiva is Tripurantaka, ender of the three cities, and his fire burns what binds.
